```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 3.4, dpi = 90)
library(varm)
source("varm-helpers.R")
set.seed(7)
y <- as.matrix(yraw)
colnames(y) <- c("inflation", "unemployment", "rate")
yr <- seq(1953, by = 0.25, length.out = nrow(y))
have_bvar <- requireNamespace("BVAR", quietly = TRUE)
```

`bvarm()` fits Bayesian VARs with two families of samplers, selected by the
`prior` argument:

| `prior =` | model | sampler | cost |
|---|---|---|---|
| `prior_minnesota()` | conjugate Normal-inverse-Wishart (NIW), Minnesota + sum-of-coefficients + single-unit-root | exact draws (fixed hyperparameters) or Metropolis for hyperparameters, then direct draws | tiny |
| `prior_triangular()` | triangular, equation-by-equation; Minnesota, SSVS or horseshoe; optional stochastic volatility | Gibbs | linear in $K$ per sweep |

Both return a `bvarm` object whose `$draws` is a `varm_draws` container, the
same one produced by the bootstrap, so `irf()`, `fevd()`, `hd()`, `forecast()`
and every identification scheme work unchanged
(see `vignette("identification")`).

## 1. The conjugate NIW posterior

Write the VAR as $Y=XB+U$, with $Y$ $T\times M$, $X$ $T\times k$ ($k=Mp+d$),
$U$ rows i.i.d. $N(0,\Sigma)$. With the conjugate prior
$$
\mathrm{vec}(B)\mid\Sigma\sim N\big(\mathrm{vec}(b),\ \Sigma\otimes\Omega\big),\qquad
\Sigma\sim IW(\Psi,\,d),\quad d=M+2,
$$
the posterior is of the same family:
\begin{align}
\mathrm{vec}(B)\mid\Sigma,Y&\sim N\big(\mathrm{vec}(\bar B),\ \Sigma\otimes\bar\Omega\big), &
\Sigma\mid Y&\sim IW(\bar\Psi,\ T+d),\\
\bar\Omega&=(X'X+\Omega^{-1})^{-1}, &
\bar B&=\bar\Omega\,(X'Y+\Omega^{-1}b),\\
\bar\Psi&=\Psi+(Y-X\bar B)'(Y-X\bar B)+(\bar B-b)'\Omega^{-1}(\bar B-b).
\end{align}
Because the posterior is available in closed form, draws for *fixed*
hyperparameters are independent (no MCMC, no burn-in). The code below
verifies the formulas against the output of `bvarm()` for a Minnesota prior
without dummy observations.

```{r niw-check}
psi <- c(0.10, 0.12, 0.67)                                  # fixed IW scale, one per variable
pr0 <- prior_minnesota(lambda = 0.2, alpha = 2, soc = NULL, sur = NULL, psi = psi, hyper = character(0))
f0  <- bvarm(y, p = 2, prior = pr0, ndraw = 20000)
p <- 2; M <- 3
Z  <- embed(y, p + 1); Yd <- Z[, 1:M]; X <- cbind(Z[, -(1:M)], const = 1)
om <- c(rep(0.2^2 / (1:p)^2, each = M) / rep(psi, p), 1e7)  # prior variance of coef of lag l, variable j: lambda^2 / (l^alpha psi_j)
b0 <- matrix(0, ncol(X), M); diag(b0[1:M, ]) <- 1           # random-walk prior mean (delta = 1)
Obar <- solve(crossprod(X) + diag(1 / om))
Bbar <- Obar %*% (crossprod(X, Yd) + diag(1 / om) %*% b0)
S    <- diag(psi) + crossprod(Yd - X %*% Bbar) + t(Bbar - b0) %*% diag(1 / om) %*% (Bbar - b0)
max(abs(coef(f0) - Bbar))                                   # posterior mean of B: Monte Carlo error only
max(abs(summary(f0)$Sigma - S / (nrow(X) + 1)))             # E[Sigma|Y] = S/(nu - M - 1), nu = T + M + 2
```

## 2. The Minnesota prior

**Prior.** The coefficient on lag $l$ of variable $j$ in equation $i$ has prior
mean $\delta_i$ if $i=j,\ l=1$ and zero otherwise, and
$$
\mathrm{Var}\big(\beta^{(l)}_{ij}\mid\Sigma\big)=\Sigma_{ii}\ \frac{\lambda^2}{l^{\alpha}\,\psi_j},
$$
while the constant has a (nearly) flat variance (`var = 1e7`). This is the
Giannone, Lenza and Primiceri (2015) parametrisation: $\Psi$ is the scale of the
inverse-Wishart (by default the AR($p$) residual variances, so that
$\psi_j$ puts variable $j$ in standard-deviation units), $\lambda$ is the
overall tightness and $\alpha$ the lag-decay exponent. The original
Litterman (1986) prior is the dummy-observation special case: the prior is
equivalent to appending artificial observations
$$
Y_d=\begin{pmatrix}\mathrm{diag}(\delta_1\sigma_1,\dots,\delta_M\sigma_M)/\lambda\\ 0\end{pmatrix},\qquad
X_d=\begin{pmatrix}\mathrm{diag}(1,2^{\alpha},\dots,p^{\alpha})\otimes\mathrm{diag}(\sigma)/\lambda & 0\\0&0\end{pmatrix}
$$
(Bańbura, Giannone and Reichlin, 2010), so the posterior mean is OLS on the augmented data.

### Economic intuition / how to use it

$\lambda$ is the prior standard deviation (in units of the residual sd) of the
first-lag coefficient on *other* variables relative to the own-lag prior
$\delta$. In words: with $\lambda\to 0$ every variable is a random walk (prior
mean $\delta=1$) and the data are ignored; $\lambda\to\infty$ is OLS. A
value around $0.2$ says "I believe each variable is mostly a random walk
with small spillovers, and spillovers die out like $l^{-\alpha}$". $\alpha=2$
says that longer lags matter quadratically less. Use `delta = 0` for series in
growth rates (prior mean white noise, not random walk).

```{r lambda, fig.height = 3.4}
ols <- coef(varm(y, p = 2))
lams <- c(0.01, 0.1, 0.2, 1, 10)
fits <- lapply(lams, function(l)
  bvarm(y, 2, prior_minnesota(lambda = l, soc = NULL, sur = NULL, hyper = character(0)), ndraw = 500))
res <- sapply(fits, function(f) c(own = coef(f)["rate.l1", "rate"], cross = coef(f)["inflation.l1", "rate"]))
colnames(res) <- paste0("lambda=", lams)
round(cbind(res, OLS = c(own = ols["rate.l1", "rate"], cross = ols["inflation.l1", "rate"])), 3)
```

The first row is the own first lag in the interest-rate equation, the second
the coefficient on lagged inflation: as $\lambda$ grows the former moves from 1
(the prior mean) to the OLS value, and the latter from 0 to OLS.

## 3. Sum-of-coefficients and single-unit-root priors

Two further dummy-observation priors, with $\bar y$ the mean of the first $p$
observations, encode beliefs about *persistence and cointegration*:

* **Sum of coefficients** (Doan, Litterman and Sims, 1984), tightness $\mu$
  (`soc`):
  $y_d=\mathrm{diag}(\bar y)/\mu$, $x_d=\big(\mathbf 1_p'\otimes \mathrm{diag}(\bar y)/\mu,\ 0\big)$.
  It says that if the average of the lags of *all* variables is constant, the
  variable stays at that level: a prior for unit roots in each variable and for no
  cointegration. $\mu\to 0$ is a VAR in differences.
* **Single unit root / dummy initial observation** (Sims, 1993), tightness
  $\theta$ (`sur`): $y_d=\bar y'/\theta$, $x_d=\big(\mathbf 1_p'\otimes\bar y'/\theta,\ 1/\theta\big)$.
  It says that the initial level is a good forecast of every variable: it
  allows cointegration, with a common stochastic trend, and shrinks
  towards it.

Pass `soc = NULL`/`sur = NULL` to drop either.

### Economic intuition / how to use it

Unit-root priors help with macro data in levels at long horizons: the OLS VAR is
biased towards stationarity, so its forecasts mean-revert too fast, and Minnesota
shrinkage alone does not correct that. They are least useful for variables
in growth rates. Whether the data want them can be read from the marginal
likelihood (next section).

## 4. Marginal likelihood and hierarchical hyperparameters

Given the NIW prior, the marginal likelihood of $Y$ is available in closed
form (with $\hat S=(Y-X\bar B)'(Y-X\bar B)+(\bar B-b)'\Omega^{-1}(\bar B-b)$):
$$
\ln p(Y\mid\theta)=-\frac{MT}{2}\ln\pi+\sum_{j=0}^{M-1}\ln\frac{\Gamma\big(\tfrac{T+d-j}{2}\big)}{\Gamma\big(\tfrac{d-j}{2}\big)}
-\frac{M}{2}\ln\big|I+\Omega^{1/2}X'X\,\Omega^{1/2}\big|+\frac d2\ln|\Psi|-\frac{T+d}{2}\ln\big|\Psi+\hat S\big|,
$$
where $\theta=(\lambda,\alpha,\mu,\theta_{sur},\psi)$. When dummy observations
are present, the likelihood of the *real* data is obtained, as in Giannone et
al. (2015), by dividing the marginal likelihood of the augmented sample
by that of the dummies alone. It is returned as `$logml`.

**Hierarchical prior.** Following Giannone, Lenza and Primiceri (2015), the
hyperparameters get their own prior (a gamma with a given `mode` and `sd`, truncated to
`[min, max]`; each is specified as `c(mode, sd, min, max)`) and are
estimated by
$$
p(\theta\mid Y)\propto p(Y\mid\theta)\,p(\theta).
$$
`bvarm()` first maximises this posterior with `optim()` (L-BFGS-B), uses the
inverse Hessian as the proposal covariance of a random-walk Metropolis
sampler (scale adapted during burn-in towards a 25-45% acceptance rate when
`adapt = TRUE`), and then draws $(B,\Sigma)$ *directly* from the NIW
posterior at each retained $\theta$. The hyperparameters estimated are listed
by `hyper` (default `c("lambda", "soc", "sur")`; `"full"` adds `alpha` and `psi`).

```{r ml-grid, fig.height = 3.6}
grid <- c(0.02, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.5, 0.8, 1.2, 2)
lml <- sapply(grid, function(l) bvarm(y, 2, prior_minnesota(lambda = l, soc = 0.3, sur = 0.4, hyper = character(0)),
                                      ndraw = 10)$logml)
par(mar = c(3.4, 3.4, 2, 0.6), mgp = c(2, 0.6, 0))
plot(grid, lml, type = "b", log = "x", pch = 16, xlab = expression(lambda), ylab = "log marginal likelihood",
     main = "Marginal likelihood as a function of overall tightness (soc = 0.3, sur = 0.4)")
abline(v = grid[which.max(lml)], lty = 2, col = "grey50")
```

```{r hier}
fit <- bvarm(y, p = 2, ndraw = 2000, nburn = 1000)
fit
fit$accept       # Metropolis acceptance rate
fit$logml        # log marginal likelihood at the hyperparameter mode
```

**Which prior does the data prefer?** The marginal likelihood compares
priors for the same data and the same $p$ (it is *not* comparable across $p$:
each $p$ drops a different number of initial observations, so the data being
explained differ).

Maximising over a grid of $\lambda$ (with $\mu=0.3$, $\theta=0.4$ when included):

```{r ml-compare}
cfg <- list(`Minnesota only`     = list(soc = NULL, sur = NULL),
            `+ sum-of-coefs`     = list(soc = 0.3, sur = NULL),
            `+ single unit root` = list(soc = NULL, sur = 0.4),
            `both`               = list(soc = 0.3, sur = 0.4))
# best log marginal likelihood over a lambda grid, hyperparameters otherwise fixed
ml <- sapply(cfg, function(a) max(sapply(grid, function(l)
  bvarm(y, 2, do.call(prior_minnesota, c(list(lambda = l, hyper = character(0)), a)), ndraw = 10)$logml)))
round(ml, 1)
```

Both dummy-observation priors raise the marginal likelihood and the
single-unit-root prior contributes most: the interest rate and unemployment
are highly persistent and the sample has few effective turning points. Since the marginal likelihood is a one-step-ahead predictive
density summed over the sample (the "Bayesian forecast-based" interpretation),
a large gain for a prior means it forecasts better *on average* over the sample, not that it is true.

### Posterior summaries, IRFs and forecasts

```{r post}
s <- summary(fit)
round(s$mean[1:3, ], 3)       # posterior means of the first-lag matrix
max(stability(fit))           # largest eigenvalue modulus across draws
ir <- irf(fit, id = id_chol(), horizon = 16)
ir
```

```{r irf-plot}
plot_irf(ir, shock = "rate")
```

The bands are *posterior credible intervals* (percentiles of the draws), not
confidence intervals. Compare with the bootstrap bands of the OLS VAR in
`vignette("var-theory")`: the Bayesian responses to the policy shock decay more
slowly and the bands are tighter because the prior shrinks the persistence
parameters towards one.

```{r fc}
fc <- forecast(fit, h = 8)
round(fc$mean, 2)
```

## 5. Triangular sampler: shrinkage priors and stochastic volatility

The conjugate prior ties the prior covariance of the coefficients in every
equation to $\Sigma$, which forces a cross-equation structure (and a symmetric
treatment of variables) and rules out stochastic volatility and
equation-specific shrinkage. The alternative (Cogley and Sargent, 2005;
Carriero, Clark and Marcellino, 2019; the `prior_triangular()` family) orthogonalises the system:
$$
A\,y_t=c+\sum_{l=1}^p\Pi_l y_{t-l}+\Lambda_t^{1/2}\varepsilon_t,\qquad
\varepsilon_t\sim N(0,I),\ \ \Lambda_t=\mathrm{diag}\big(e^{h_{1t}},\dots,e^{h_{Kt}}\big),
$$
with $A$ unit lower triangular. Equation $i$ is a *regression* of $y_{it}$ on
the lags, the constant and the contemporaneous $y_{1t},\dots,y_{i-1,t}$, with
(conditionally) independent equations, so each Gibbs sweep costs
$O(K(Kp)^3)$ rather than $O((K^2p)^3)$ for the joint system. The reduced form is
$B=\Pi' A'^{-1}$ and $\Sigma_t=A^{-1}\Lambda_tA^{-1\prime}$.
These draws are stored as reduced-form $(B,\Sigma)$ pairs and mapped through
the same identification code.

**Prior variances.** With $s_i$ the AR residual standard deviation,
the base variance of the coefficient on lag $l$ of variable $j$ in
equation $i$ is $s_i^2/(s_j^2\,l^{\alpha})$, multiplied by

* `type = "minnesota"`: $\lambda_1^2$ for own lags and $\lambda_1^2\lambda_2^2$ for other
  variables (cross-variable shrinkage);
* `type = "ssvs"` (George, Sun and Ni, 2008): $\lambda_1^2$ (slab) when an inclusion indicator
  $\gamma_{ij}=1$ and $\rho^2\lambda_1^2$ (spike) otherwise, with
  $\Pr(\gamma_{ij}=1)=$ `inclusion`;
* `type = "horseshoe"` (Carvalho, Polson and Scott, 2010; Makalic and Schmidt, 2016): $\tau_i^2\lambda_{ij}^2$ with
  half-Cauchy global ($\tau_i$) and local ($\lambda_{ij}$) scales, sampled via
  inverse-gamma mixtures: aggressive shrinkage of noise coefficients and almost
  no shrinkage of large ones.

The contemporaneous coefficients $a_{ij}$ get a prior sd of $\lambda_5 s_i/s_j$
and the constants of $\lambda_3 s_i$.

```{r tri}
fm <- bvarm(y, p = 4, prior = prior_triangular("minnesota"), ndraw = 1000, nburn = 500)
fs <- bvarm(y, p = 4, prior = prior_triangular("ssvs"),      ndraw = 1000, nburn = 500)
fh <- bvarm(y, p = 4, prior = prior_triangular("horseshoe"), ndraw = 1000, nburn = 500)
fm
```

### SSVS inclusion probabilities and the horseshoe

`$inclusion` holds the posterior probability that each lag coefficient
belongs to the slab. Rows are the regressors in the same order as
`coef()` (lag 1 of each variable, lag 2, ...), columns the equations.

```{r ssvs}
inc <- fs$inclusion
dimnames(inc) <- list(rownames(coef(fs))[1:12], colnames(y))
round(inc[1:6, ], 2)             # lags 1 and 2
```

The coefficients that matter (own first lags, the first lag of unemployment in
the inflation and rate equations, and the second lag of inflation in its own
equation) have inclusion probabilities near 1. Many other cross-variable and
higher-lag coefficients end up at or below the prior value of 0.5, i.e. the data do not
support keeping them.
Shrinkage priors earn their keep when the lag length $p$ or the number of
variables $K$ is large. Posterior mean coefficients across the three priors
(equation `rate`, second lag block):

```{r shrink-compare}
round(cbind(minnesota = coef(fm)[5:7, "rate"], ssvs = coef(fs)[5:7, "rate"],
            horseshoe = coef(fh)[5:7, "rate"]), 3)
dim(fh$tau)                      # horseshoe global scale per equation, per draw
```

### Ordering caveat

Because equation $i$ conditions on $y_1,\dots,y_{i-1}$, the *prior*
(not the likelihood) depends on the order of the variables: shrinkage on
$\Pi$ is applied to a rotated system. The differences are not negligible
(compare with posterior standard deviations before dismissing them); check by
reordering the data:

```{r order}
f1 <- bvarm(y,            p = 2, prior = prior_triangular("minnesota"), ndraw = 1000, nburn = 500)
f2 <- bvarm(y[, 3:1],     p = 2, prior = prior_triangular("minnesota"), ndraw = 1000, nburn = 500)
b1 <- coef(f1); b2 <- coef(f2)[rownames(b1), colnames(b1)]
round(b1 - b2, 2)           # posterior-mean difference between the two orderings
```

Order the variables as in a recursive identification (slowest-moving first),
which is also what the triangular sampler is naturally suited to. A
"Cholesky" structural analysis of this sampler is consistent with its
parametrisation.

### Stochastic volatility

With `sv = TRUE` each log-variance follows a random walk,
$h_{it}=h_{i,t-1}+\nu_{it}$, $\nu_{it}\sim N(0,\sigma^2_{h,i})$, with an
inverse-gamma$(a,b)$ prior on $\sigma_{h,i}^2$ and initial variance $V_0$
(`sv_prior = c(a = 5, b = 0.04, V0 = 10)`; prior mean of $\sigma_h^2$ is $b/(a-1)=0.01$).
Writing $\tilde y_{it}=\ln(\varepsilon_{it}^2\lambda_{it}+c)$ with
$\varepsilon_{it}$ the equation residual, the model is linear in $h_{it}$ with a
$\log\chi^2_1$ error, which Kim, Shephard and Chib (1998) (and Omori et al., 2007)
approximate by a 10-component Gaussian mixture. Given the mixture
indicators, $h_{i\cdot}$ is drawn jointly by forward-filtering,
backward-sampling (Carter and Kohn, 1994; Frühwirth-Schnatter, 1994), then
$\sigma_{h,i}^2$ from its inverse-gamma conditional.

```{r sv, fig.height = 3.6}
t_sv <- system.time(fsv <- bvarm(y, p = 2, prior = prior_triangular("minnesota"), ndraw = 1000, nburn = 1000, sv = TRUE))
v <- volatility(fsv)                       # posterior-mean standard deviation of each structural shock
yrv <- yr[-(1:2)]
par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(3, 3, 2, 0.6), mgp = c(1.7, 0.5, 0))
for (j in 1:3) { plot(yrv, v[, j], type = "l", lwd = 2, col = "firebrick", xlab = "", ylab = "", main = colnames(y)[j])
                 abline(v = 1984, lty = 3, col = "grey50") }
round(cbind(`pre-1984` = colMeans(v[yrv < 1984, ]), `post-1984` = colMeans(v[yrv >= 1984, ])), 3)
```

### Economic intuition / how to use it

* **When SV matters.** The Great Moderation after the early 1980s lowered the
  volatility of all three series (the dotted line marks 1984; the
  post-1984 average standard deviation of all three structural shocks is
  35-45% lower). A constant-variance VAR averages two regimes: it
  overstates uncertainty in the moderation and understates it before.
  Density forecasts and the *scale* of IRFs change; the *shape* of IRFs
  (the dynamics) is unchanged because $B$ is constant. SV is therefore
  mainly a gain for predictive densities and for correct structural scaling.
* **2020.** The Covid episode in 2020 has outliers hundreds of times larger than
  usual. A random-walk volatility absorbs them only slowly and leaves
  volatility elevated for years, so predictive intervals after 2020 are too wide for
  too long (Lenza and Primiceri, 2022). The sample here ends in 2006 and the
  current release has no outlier-robust (e.g. $t$ or outlier-mixture)
  variants: for 2020-21 data, drop or dummy the pandemic quarters, or
  treat results with caution.
* **IRFs under SV.** The reduced-form covariance varies in time. `irf()` uses
  by default `vol = "last"`, the covariance at the end of the sample
  (a low-volatility date here), whereas `vol = "mean"` uses the posterior
  mean covariance: the size of the shock differs by a factor of two.

```{r sv-irf}
i_last <- irf(fsv, horizon = 12, vol = "last")
i_mean <- irf(fsv, horizon = 12, vol = "mean")
round(c(last = i_last$estimate["rate", "rate", 1], mean = i_mean$estimate["rate", "rate", 1]), 3)
```

Normalise with `normalise = list(shock = "rate", variable = "rate", size = 1)`
to compare shapes across volatility dates. Forecasts from an SV fit simulate
the volatility forward as a random walk, so the predictive density widens
with the horizon even when the VAR is stationary.

## 6. Convergence checks

The conjugate sampler at fixed hyperparameters needs no diagnostics (draws are
i.i.d.). Everything else is MCMC. Minimal checks, with base graphics:

1. **Acceptance rate** of the hyperparameter Metropolis sampler (`fit$accept`;
   aim at 0.2-0.45).
2. **Trace and autocorrelation** of the hyperparameter draws.
3. **Effective sample size** and **split $\hat R$** from two chains
   started at different seeds.

```{r conv, fig.height = 3.6}
ess <- function(x) {                       # initial-positive-sequence ESS
  a <- acf(x, lag.max = min(500, length(x) - 1), plot = FALSE)$acf[-1]
  k <- which(a < 0)[1]; if (is.na(k)) k <- length(a)
  length(x) / (1 + 2 * sum(a[seq_len(k - 1)]))
}
rhat <- function(chains) {                 # split R-hat on a list of equal-length chains
  ch <- unlist(lapply(chains, function(x) { m <- length(x) %/% 2; list(x[1:m], x[m + 1:m]) }), recursive = FALSE)
  n <- length(ch[[1]]); W <- mean(sapply(ch, var)); B <- n * var(sapply(ch, mean))
  sqrt(((n - 1) / n * W + B / n) / W)
}
set.seed(11); c1 <- bvarm(y, p = 2, ndraw = 2000, nburn = 1000)
set.seed(12); c2 <- bvarm(y, p = 2, ndraw = 2000, nburn = 1000)
c(accept1 = c1$accept, accept2 = c2$accept)
# effective sample sizes out of 2000 retained draws: use longer runs for tail quantiles
round(rbind(ESS = apply(c1$hyper, 2, ess),
            Rhat = sapply(colnames(c1$hyper), function(h) rhat(list(c1$hyper[, h], c2$hyper[, h])))), 3)
par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(3, 3, 2, 0.6), mgp = c(1.7, 0.5, 0))
plot(c1$hyper[, "lambda"], type = "l", col = "grey40", main = "trace: lambda", xlab = "", ylab = "")
lines(c2$hyper[, "lambda"], col = adjustcolor("firebrick", 0.6))
acf(c1$hyper[, "lambda"], main = "ACF: lambda", lag.max = 40)
plot(cumsum(c1$hyper[, "lambda"]) / seq_len(2000), type = "l", main = "running mean: lambda", xlab = "", ylab = "")
```

For the triangular sampler, `thin` reduces storage but not the work; inspect
traces of the quantities you care about (an impulse response at a given
horizon, the volatility at a given date, the SSVS inclusion
probabilities) rather than of thousands of coefficients. SV and
shrinkage hyperparameters are the slowest mixing, so use a longer `nburn` for
them.

```{r conv-sv}
ir_sv <- sapply(1:2, function(k) {
  set.seed(20 + k)
  f <- bvarm(y, p = 2, prior = prior_triangular("minnesota"), ndraw = 1000, nburn = 1000, sv = TRUE)
  irf(f, horizon = 8, vol = "mean", normalise = list(shock = "rate", variable = "rate", size = 1),
      level = 0.9)$estimate["unemployment", "rate", 5]
})
round(ir_sv, 3)    # posterior median response at horizon 4 from two independent chains
```

## 7. Speed

All sampling loops are compiled. Wall-clock time (seconds, your machine
will differ) for a `K = 3`, `p = 4` model:

```{r speed}
tm <- function(expr) unname(system.time(expr)[["elapsed"]])
tab <- c(
  `NIW, fixed hyperparameters (5000 draws)`      = tm(bvarm(y, 4, prior_minnesota(hyper = character(0)), ndraw = 5000)),
  `NIW, hierarchical (3000 draws + 1000 burn-in)` = tm(bvarm(y, 4, ndraw = 3000, nburn = 1000)),
  `triangular Minnesota (2000 sweeps)`           = tm(bvarm(y, 4, prior_triangular("minnesota"), ndraw = 1500, nburn = 500)),
  `triangular SSVS (2000 sweeps)`                = tm(bvarm(y, 4, prior_triangular("ssvs"), ndraw = 1500, nburn = 500)),
  `triangular horseshoe (2000 sweeps)`           = tm(bvarm(y, 4, prior_triangular("horseshoe"), ndraw = 1500, nburn = 500)),
  `triangular + SV (2000 sweeps)`                = tm(bvarm(y, 4, prior_triangular("minnesota"), ndraw = 1500, nburn = 500, sv = TRUE)))
round(tab, 2)
```

## 8. Comparison with the BVAR package

The `BVAR` package (Kuschnig and Vashold, 2021) implements the same
hierarchical Minnesota/SOC/SUR prior. A like-for-like comparison needs one
caveat: **the default scale $\Psi$ differs**. `BVAR` chooses the inverse-Wishart
scale $\psi$ from its own "auto" rule (here roughly 3 times larger for
inflation and unemployment and 1.2 times for the interest rate than the AR($p$)
residual variances used by `bvarm()`), which in turn changes the posterior of $\lambda$. Passing the same
$\psi$ to both gives matching results:

```{r bvar-pkg, eval = have_bvar}
b <- BVAR::bvar(y, lags = 2, n_draw = 12000, n_burn = 3000, n_thin = 4L, verbose = FALSE,
                priors = BVAR::bv_priors(hyper = c("lambda", "soc", "sur"),
                                         mn = BVAR::bv_mn(lambda = BVAR::bv_lambda(mode = 0.2, sd = 0.4, min = 1e-4, max = 5)),
                                         soc = BVAR::bv_soc(), sur = BVAR::bv_sur()))
psi_b <- b$priors$psi$mode                                # BVAR's own default scale
f_def <- bvarm(y, 2, ndraw = 3000, nburn = 1000)           # varm default scale (AR(p) variances)
f_eq  <- bvarm(y, 2, prior_minnesota(psi = psi_b), ndraw = 3000, nburn = 1000)
t_v <- tm(bvarm(y, 2, prior_minnesota(psi = psi_b), ndraw = 3000, nburn = 1000))
t_b <- tm(BVAR::bvar(y, lags = 2, n_draw = 4000, n_burn = 1000, verbose = FALSE))
hy <- rbind(`varm, default psi`   = colMeans(f_def$hyper),
            `varm, BVAR psi`      = colMeans(f_eq$hyper),
            `BVAR`                = colMeans(b$hyper[, c("lambda", "soc", "sur")]))
round(hy, 3)
```

```{r bvar-irf, eval = have_bvar}
ib <- BVAR::irf(b, BVAR::bv_irf(horizon = 17, identification = TRUE), n_thin = 1L)
mb <- apply(ib$irf, c(2, 3, 4), median)                   # [response, horizon, shock]
iv <- irf(f_eq, horizon = 16)
cmp <- rbind(varm = iv$estimate["unemployment", "rate", c(1, 5, 9, 17)],
             BVAR = mb[2, c(1, 5, 9, 17), 3])
colnames(cmp) <- paste0("h=", c(0, 4, 8, 16))
round(cmp, 3)                                            # same Cholesky ordering, one-sd shock
round(c(`varm seconds` = t_v, `BVAR seconds` = t_b), 2)
```

What to take from this comparison. (i) With the same prior inputs the two
implementations agree on the IRFs to about the second decimal and on the
hyperparameter posterior means within Monte Carlo error, which validates the NIW
code. (ii) The default $\psi$ is a *modelling*
choice with a visible effect on $\lambda$; check it before comparing numbers
across packages. (iii) `varm` is faster in wall-clock time; part of this is the compiled
sampler, part the adaptive proposal (acceptance 25-45% against a lower rate
for `BVAR`'s default), so each retained draw is worth more. Compare effective
sample sizes, not nominal draws. (iv) `BVAR` offers features not (yet) in `varm`,
such as conditional forecasts and a richer set of hyperparameters (see
`vignette("choosing-a-method")`).
